source.title: Training on the Test Task Confounds Evaluation and Emergence
source.authors: Ricardo Dominguez-Olmedo; Florian E. Dorner; Moritz Hardt

record.tranche_reason: The study's own experiments refine claims about downstream scaling and emergence: benchmark-accuracy scaling fits and emergence points change with task-specific fine-tuning and evaluation format. It does not test held-out pretraining cross-entropy laws or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The study measures downstream benchmark accuracy against estimated pretraining compute, not held-out cross-entropy loss. It does not test architecture-shape effects or validate extrapolations from small runs to much larger ones. The reported pretraining token counts and parameter counts are used to estimate compute, not as separate loss-scaling outcomes. Rows below capture the downstream scaling and fit-dependence results, including the reported aggregate regression and emergence-fit statistics.
record.test_reason: The study's own results on 56 base models (70M–70B) bear on V6. Benchmark accuracy versus estimated pretraining compute (C≈6ND) fits a log-linear trend well only after all models get the same task fine-tuning. Without it, models trained after Nov 2023 score 7 (MMLU) and 19 (GSM8K) points higher at equal compute, and accuracy stays near chance until about 1e22 FLOPs. This argues that downstream predictability from scale needs qualifying, by training-data exposure to the test task and by evaluation format. No held-out loss, allocation or architecture-shape results are reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that training on the test task (e.g., instruction data or MCQA-style data in pretraining) explains most of newer models' advantage per unit of compute and confounds model comparisons. Fine-tuning all models on the same sufficient task data equalizes them and restores cleaner log-linear scaling with pretraining compute. Emergence shifts to smaller scales and gradually disappears with more task training, even where switching to a continuous metric does not remove it.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes downstream benchmark accuracy versus estimated pretraining compute and fine-tunes models on task-relevant data; it does not reproduce held-out cross-entropy scaling-law measurements or compute-optimal allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported emergence point and fit quality vary with the amount of task-specific fine-tuning. The paper also reports differences in apparent emergence across evaluation formats and metrics, including cloze versus multiple-choice evaluation and accuracy versus Brier score.
record.problems: The evidence concerns benchmark accuracy rather than held-out pretraining loss. Pretraining compute is estimated from parameter and token counts. Fine-tuning is used as an intervention on task exposure, so the observed fit changes are specific to that downstream setting; the paper also notes the cost of fine-tuning and the possible difficulty of obtaining task-relevant data.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute is not measured.
No compute-optimal allocation experiments. Over-trained small models matching larger ones is only remarked on.
No depth or width comparisons at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities and no repeated-data regimes. Fine-tuning is used as an intervention on downstream accuracy, not as a loss-scaling regime.
Downstream performance versus pretraining loss (only estimated compute is used). Extrapolation of downstream fits to larger scales.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal split on parameter counting, schedule or fitting method is not tested.

missing.what: ARC and HellaSwag under cloze versus multiple-choice: θ, smooth scaling versus emergence at 1e22–1e23 FLOPs, and Brier-score results
MMLU cloze (θ=0.008) and Brier score still showing sharp improvement between 1e22 and 1e23 FLOPs
Instruction and chat models: MMLU R² 0.950 (gap 0.063) and GSM8K R² 0.841 (gap 0.154); after adjustment R² 0.983 and 0.929
Leaderboard v2 benchmarks (MMLU Pro, GPQA, BBH, MuSR, MATH Lvl5): cohort gaps at equal compute and their reduction after adjustment
Robustness of cohort gap and R² to the temporal cutoff and to an EN versus EN+CN split

record.verdict_notes: V7 was removed from all rows. It concerns loss-law exponents and the compute-optimal split, while these rows are downstream accuracy fits; their fit-dependence is recorded as V6 scope limits instead. In r5–r12, ce comes from the piecewise fit and R² from a separate pure log-linear fit. Compute is estimated as 6ND across heterogeneous model families, not from controlled runs.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute.
No validation that power laws fitted on small runs predict the loss of much larger runs.
No compute-budget comparison of parameter/token allocations or fitted allocation exponents.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The experiments concern text-language-model benchmark evaluation; no other modality or the listed alternative training regimes are tested.
The study measures benchmark accuracy against estimated pretraining compute, not downstream performance against pretraining loss. It does not establish small-run-to-large-run extrapolation.

The study shows effects of task-specific fine-tuning and evaluation format on downstream accuracy fits and emergence. It does not test parameter-counting conventions, compute-optimal allocation, or compare alternative fitting methods for the original held-out-loss laws.

tranche.reason: The study shows that downstream predictability requires qualification by task exposure and evaluation format.

source_check.notes: Figure 1 R² includes a cohort indicator and emergence knot; Figures 9/20 report R² from separate pure log-linear fits. The supplied source is the April 2025 v3; its text does not establish the pack's ICLR 2024 review metadata.

statements.correction: V6 limits_scope for released-model comparisons with uncontrolled task exposure; V6 supports after common sufficient task fine-tuning. Figure 1 cohort differences: MMLU 0.073→0.005; GSM8K 0.191→0.005.
statements.problem: The study-specific sentence is accurate, but its challenges placement overstates the evidence: scaling remains positive and becomes more predictable after controlling task exposure.
